title: kv-cache-offload-paging-design-draft-v2
content:
Status: DRAFT (v2)
Author: Leah Chen (eng-serving-runtime)
Reviewers: Ravi Iyer, Sofia Martinez, Daniel Park
Summary:
This draft defines a multi-tier KV cache offload and host-paging strategy for the serving runtime. It covers PCIe-hosted RAM offload, NUMA/UMA considerations, NVMe-backed cold storage, thresholds and heuristics for eviction/prefetch, and interactions with scheduling and kernel selection. Primary goal is to reduce GPU memory pressure while preserving latency SLOs for tail and p50/p95.

Goals:
- Enable large-context models to run under constrained GPU memory by transparently offloading less-recent KV shards to host RAM and, optionally, NVMe.
- Maintain latency SLOs: prioritize p50/p95 and bound p99 tail behavior for interactive workloads.
- Integrate with existing batching and scheduling so offload decisions are workload-aware.
- Provide observability and tunable policies (thresholds, prefetch windows).

Constraints and assumptions:
- PCIe Gen4/5 bandwidth and latency characteristics are assumed; specific numbers to be validated per instance family.
- Hosts may be UMA or NUMA; memory access latency to GPU-visible host RAM varies.
- NVMe (local) used only as cold backing store for very large KV sets or long-tail sequences; not for hot-path serving.
- Offload operations should be asynchronous and overlapped with computation whenever possible.

High-level architecture:
Tier 0: On-GPU KV cache (hot) — fastest, stored in device DRAM, used for immediate attention.
Tier 1: Host RAM (pinned, page-locked when necessary) over PCIe — medium latency, used for warm entries.
Tier 2: Local NVMe swap (optionally DAX if supported) — cold storage for long tail, highest latency.

Key design elements:
1) Offload unit and shard granularity
- Unit: contiguous KV blocks aligned to attention layer boundaries (per-layer per-head KV chunks).
- Shard size: tuneable, default 4–16MB to balance PCIe transfer startup overhead vs granularity for partial fetch.

2) Placement and NUMA/UMA awareness
- Host memory allocation is NUMA-aware. For GPUs attached to a specific NUMA node, prefer allocations on the same node to reduce host->GPU copy latency.
- On systems with UMA (e.g., certain cloud instances), fall back to generic allocations but track access latency in telemetry.
- Maintain per-GPU host RAM pools with soft quotas to prevent host memory exhaustion.

3) Eviction, promotion, and thresholds
- Idle threshold: an entry not referenced for T_idle ms becomes eligible for demotion from GPU->host. Default T_idle = 200ms (interactive); configurable per workload.
- Host eviction threshold: when host pool exceeds H_pct (default 75% of configured pool), apply LRU-based eviction to NVMe or free memory.
- GPU eviction policy: LRU + recency weighted by sequence stripe and model layer importance. Model layers closer to output (higher layers) get a slight promotion bias.
- Promotion: on access miss in GPU but hit in host, asynchronously schedule DMA to GPU; if request latency budget allows, block the token generation until DMA completes; otherwise use a degraded fallback kernel (see kernels section).

4) Prefetching heuristics
- Request-aware prefetch: for autoregressive workloads, prefetch next K steps of KV for active sequences when predicted probability of continuation exceeds P_prefetch (default 0.2).
- Batch-aware prefetch: when batching multiple sequences, prefetch KV for top-N highest-probability continuations across batch.
- Idle-window prefetch: during GPU compute stalls (e.g., kernel on-board compute), perform background prefetch of likely-needed KV.

5) DMA and PCIe usage patterns
- Use large contiguous DMA transfers where possible to amortize PCIe startup cost.
- Prefer pinned host memory and use GPUDirect/peer mechanisms when available to reduce copy steps.
- Rate-limit in-flight DMA transfers per GPU to avoid saturating PCIe and interfering with other traffic (default max_concurrent_transfers = 4, configurable).

6) NVMe-backed cold store behavior
- NVMe used only when host RAM pool crosses the H_pct eviction threshold or when configured in long-history workloads.
- Use asynchronous I/O with aligned writes and large block sizes to reduce latency variance.
- Provide an optional compaction job to merge small KV fragments on NVMe to improve read throughput.

7) Interaction with scheduling and kernel selection
- Scheduler must be informed of anticipated DMA needs for scheduled workloads. Jobs with high offload rate should be scheduled with headroom to overlap DMA with compute.
- Kernel selection: when a requested KV shard is unavailable on GPU and DMA would violate latency budget, use a fallback kernel that:
  a) Recomputes partial attention by truncating KV (approximate attention) OR
  b) Uses a smoothed attention cache derived from previous steps (approximate but fast)
- Prefer kernel that degrades gracefully with a measurable quality metric so Optimize can track regressions.

8) Telemetry and SLOs
- Metrics to export per request and per model: KV_hit_rate_gpu, KV_hit_rate_host, avg_offload_latency_ms, dma_bandwidth_utilization, host_pool_usage_bytes, nvme_io_latency_ms.
- SLO probe: p50/p95/p99 generation latency with tag for whether any offload/DMA occurred.
- Alerts: host_pool_usage > 90% for >1m; sustained dma_bandwidth_utilization > 80% for >2m; KV_host_miss_rate rising > 10% indicating misconfigured thresholds.

9) Configuration knobs
- T_idle (ms) for GPU->host demotion.
- host_pool_size (bytes) per GPU node.
- H_pct threshold for NVMe eviction.
- max_concurrent_transfers per GPU.
- prefetch_window (steps) and P_prefetch.
- policy presets: interactive_low_memory, throughput_batched, long_history_offload.

10) Safety and resource governance
- Soft quotas and admission control: when host pools are full and NVMe exhausted, apply backpressure to scheduler to reduce concurrency or reject new long-history requests.
- Per-tenant limits to avoid noisy-neighbor effects in Dedicated/Private deployments.

Implementation roadmap & rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (prototype): implement host RAM offload with simple LRU demotion, pinned allocations, single-GPU testing, basic telemetry.
- Phase 1 (v1): NUMA-aware allocations, prefetch heuristics, concurrency limits, scheduler integration hooks, fallback kernel.
- Phase 2 (v2): NVMe cold-store integration, compaction job, multi-GPU coherence for shared KV sets, configurable policy presets.
- Phase 3: production hardening, per-tenant quotas, Optimize integration for automated threshold tuning.

Performance experiments to run (initial):
- Microbenchmarks: DMA latency vs transfer size on representative instance types (PCIe Gen4/5).
- End-to-end: p50/p95/p99 for GPT-style model with context lengths {1k, 8k, 32k} under offload vs no-offload.
- Stress: concurrent clients generating many long-history sequences to test host pool and NVMe eviction behavior.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default shard size: 4MB vs 16MB tradeoffs across instance types. Need empirical data.
- Fallback kernel selection: prefer truncated-attention vs smoothed-cache; requires quality regressions evaluation.
- NVMe DAX vs buffered I/O: dependent on instance support.
- Admission control strategy during contention: throttle vs reject vs degrade quality.

Appendix: implementation notes
- Tie into existing KV cache metadata store; add state bits: HOT_ON_GPU, WARM_ON_HOST, COLD_ON_NVME, IN_FLIGHT_DMA.
- Use bounded async work queues per GPU for DMA ops; prioritize foreground requests over background prefetch.
- Ensure correctness for multi-streamed sequence generation: maintain per-sequence pinned references to prevent premature eviction during in-flight generation.

Next steps:
- Assign microbench ownership: Ravi (PCIe microbench), Sofia (NUMA tests and allocation), Daniel (prefetch heuristics).
- Schedule workshop to pick shard defaults and run first set of experiments (target by 2026-03-15).

Comments and feedback welcome.
